title: Listening in Devgandhari
hook: a short hymn sounds bleak the first time; the second time, you hear where it ends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Devgandhari, and your line was one word: gentle. When you slipped, could you answer yourself the way you'd answer a friend? Day one thousand seventy-seven.

A text message arrives: we need to talk. Read it once, fast, and it can sound like trouble. Read it again, slowly, and you notice the little smile emoji at the end. Same words. Different message. Speed changes what we hear. Short pieces are the easiest to rush, because they're over before we've arrived. Devgandhari is a short section of the Granth, and the hymn we're hearing from it today is short too. They reward the opposite of rushing. Today: listening in Devgandhari.
screen: `READ ONCE, FAST.` → `READ AGAIN, SLOWLY.` → `SHORT THINGS GET RUSHED.`

segments.voice: Take one of Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Devgandhari. Hear it once, quickly, and here's roughly what lands, in plain English: in this world I have seen that love is false. Everyone is attached to their own comfort, whether spouse or friend. Everyone says mine, mine, and binds the heart to self-interest. At the end, no one goes along. It sounds bleak. A first listen might stop right there and file it under gloomy. Now hear it again, slowly. The hymn speaks to the foolish mind that still doesn't understand, though the Guru keeps teaching it. That's yesterday's gentleness, the patient voice. And then the last line, the one a rushed ear misses: Nanak says the one who sings the songs of God crosses the fearful ocean. The hymn doesn't end in the dark. It ends on singing, which is exactly what the listener is hearing at that moment. That turn takes a second, slower listening to catch. A short hymn can seem like a single mood. Heard slowly, this one has a shape: a hard look at things, a patient word to the mind, and a turn toward the Name. The Guru set this one in a gentle raga, so even the hard opening is sung softly, and the singing carries you to the end. So today's practice is plain. Listen twice. The first time, let the words go by. The second time, slowly, listen for where the hymn ends up. That's today's line: twice, slowly.
screen: `FIRST LISTEN: LOVE IS FALSE.` · `MINE, MINE, AND NO ONE GOES ALONG.` · `SECOND LISTEN: THE LAST LINE.` · `SINGING GOD'S SONGS CARRIES ACROSS.` · then, large: `TWICE, SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow second hearing. Sit, and breathe. Bring back one sentence from today, any you remember: everyone says mine, mine, or the one who sings crosses over. Say it once in your head at normal speed. Then say it again, half as fast, letting each word land before the next one starts. Notice which word gets heavier the second time. Stay with that word. If you pray, you can let it lead into Waheguru. If you don't, simply stay with the word. Later, play one Devgandhari hymn twice in a row, the second time with nothing else open. The bell holds the time.
Listening in Devgandhari. Short hymns heard twice, slowly, so the turn at the end isn't missed. Today's word.
Your line: twice, slowly. Today, read one message twice before you answer it, and see whether the second reading changes your reply. Day one thousand seventy-seven.

howItsDone: In kirtan, ragis return to a shabad's refrain line between verses, so the listener hears its center again and again; Guru Tegh Bahadur's Devgandhari hymns are sung in that gentle raga.
